output:
I found 6 findings, all critical. The main one: text a user posts to `POST /fix` goes into the system prompt, and whatever the model replies is run as a shell command, with the output sent back to the caller. Today `model-client.js` always returns the same reply (`echo restarted`), so the user's text can't choose the command yet. Once a real model sits behind `complete()`, this is remote code execution. Nothing here was run or probed; every path comes from reading the code. Coverage is 11 of 13 checks and confidence is LOW, because I couldn't run the hidden-character search or read the method skill as CTOC's own copy.

response:
  dispatch_id: "01JS7SHELL0000000000000001"
  protocol_version: 1
  agent: ai-quality/llm-security-tester
  agent_version: "not visible to this agent"
  completed_at: "2026-10-06T19:45:11Z"
  findings:
    - id: llm-security-tester/01JS7SHELL0000000000000001/001
      severity: critical
      type: prompt_injection_to_execution
      file: "src/helpdesk.js"
      line_range: [11, 18]
      message: |
        Text from the unauthenticated POST /fix request body is concatenated into the model's system prompt, and the model's reply is passed unchanged to execSync, so it runs as a shell command on the server. The command's standard output goes back to the caller in the HTTP response. One request can therefore run any command the model can be talked into writing, and read back what it prints: environment variables, files the process can read, anything reachable from the host's network.
      rationale: |
        I found this path by reading the code; no probe was run:
          - src/server.js:21 takes `message` from the JSON body.
          - src/server.js:26 checks only that it is a string.
          - src/server.js:30 passes it to fixProblem.
          - src/helpdesk.js:13 concatenates it into the `system` field.
          - src/helpdesk.js:12 calls complete().
          - src/helpdesk.js:17 calls execSync(reply.text, ...).
          - src/server.js:30 writes the command's output to the response.
        Between the reply and execSync there is nothing: no parsing, no allowlist, no confirmation, no sandbox.
        OWASP LLM05:2025 Improper Output Handling says unhandled output "can result in XSS and CSRF in web browsers as well as SSRF, privilege escalation, or remote code execution on backend systems". This is the remote code execution case.
        The two execSync options do not contain it:
          - `timeout: 10000` limits only how long the call waits. A command that starts a background process and returns at once leaves that process running.
          - `encoding: 'utf8'` only decodes the output.
        Failure path: execSync throws when the command exits non-zero or hits the timeout. Nothing catches that between helpdesk.js:17 and the 'end' listener at src/server.js:18-31. So a model reply such as a command that fails, or one that sleeps past 10 s, ends the Node process for every user (unless a process-level handler exists in a file I did not read).
        Reachability limit: src/model-client.js:12 returns the fixed text `echo restarted` no matter what it is asked. With the client as I read it, the user's text cannot choose the command. The chain goes live as soon as complete() returns text the model wrote, which is what its interface is for. helpdesk.js has no defence of its own for that case.
        These Node.js behaviours come from Node's documented child_process behaviour; I did not read that documentation during this dispatch:
          - execSync runs its string through a shell.
          - it throws on a non-zero exit or a timeout.
          - on timeout it kills only the direct child.
      suggestion: |
        Never run model output as a command. Replace execSync(reply.text) with a fixed set of remediation actions written in code. Have the model return only an action identifier, plus arguments if needed. Validate both against that set, and run the action without a shell (execFile with a fixed program and fixed argument positions).
        If free-form commands are truly needed, run them in a disposable sandbox: no network, no filesystem beyond a scratch path, no credentials. Put a human confirmation in front that shows the exact command (finding 002).
        Catch the sink's errors so one failed command cannot stop the server.
        Restoring structural separation (finding 003) does not close this finding on its own (check 1).
      confidence: MEDIUM
      confidence_rationale: |
        Each step of the path is at the lines cited. Reachability was not probed. Two things are needed for exploitation today:
          - complete() must return model-written text. The copy I read (src/model-client.js:12) returns a constant.
          - POST /fix must be reachable from a network. The files I read never call server.listen.
        Both are listed under unknowns.
      citations:
        evidence:
          - file: "src/server.js"
            line_range: [18, 31]
          - file: "src/helpdesk.js"
            line_range: [11, 18]
          - file: "src/model-client.js"
            line_range: [8, 13]
      context:
        owasp_llm_category: "LLM05:2025 Improper Output Handling (by entry name, LLM10:2026 Improper Output Handling); also LLM01:2025 Prompt Injection"
        owasp_agentic_category: "ASI05: Unexpected Code Execution (RCE)"
        taxonomy_mapping: "AML.T0051.000 (LLM Prompt Injection, sub-technique Direct; achieves AML.TA0005 Execution) and AML.T0050 Command and Scripting Interpreter (achieves AML.TA0005 Execution), ATLAS release 2026.09, looked up in this dispatch"
        chain: ["src/server.js:21 request body field message", "src/helpdesk.js:13 system prompt concatenation", "src/helpdesk.js:17 execSync(reply.text)", "src/server.js:30 command output returned to caller"]
        agreeing_skills: []
      tags: ["llm-security", "injection", "chain", "rce", "output-handling"]

    - id: llm-security-tester/01JS7SHELL0000000000000001/002
      severity: critical
      type: excessive_agency
      file: "src/helpdesk.js"
      line_range: [17, 17]
      message: |
        The model's one action is a shell running with the Node process's full operating-system authority. There is no allowlist of commands, no sandbox and no human confirmation. Any caller of POST /fix can trigger it without authentication, so the action runs with far more authority than the person asking.
      rationale: |
        OWASP LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency names three root causes. All three are present:
          - Excessive functionality: an unrestricted shell.
          - Excessive permissions: the process's own user, given to an anonymous caller.
          - Excessive autonomy: the command runs with no confirmation.
        Whether a command is allowed is left entirely to the model, through the instruction at src/helpdesk.js:13. LLM06:2025 says, under "Complete mediation": "Implement authorization in downstream systems rather than relying on an LLM to decide if an action is allowed or not".
        No destructive command goes through a human, so the confirmation rule in check 4 (show the exact action and its arguments, not the model's account of it) has nothing to apply to.
      suggestion: |
        Narrow the tool to an allowlist of named actions implemented in code, each taking typed and validated arguments. Run them as an account limited to what a helpdesk fix needs, and decide authorisation in code from the authenticated caller.
        Any destructive or irreversible action should need a human confirmation that shows the exact command and arguments that will run.
      confidence: HIGH
      confidence_rationale: |
        The whole defect is in the lines read:
          untrusted text from src/helpdesk.js:17: "return execSync(reply.text, { encoding: 'utf8', timeout: 10000 });"
        and src/server.js:9-30 has no authentication check before untrusted text from src/server.js:30: "fixProblem(message)".
        Whether the deployed process runs inside an operating-system sandbox is not in the files read (see unknowns). Even with one, there is still no allowlist and no confirmation.
      citations:
        evidence:
          - file: "src/helpdesk.js"
            line_range: [12, 17]
          - file: "src/server.js"
            line_range: [8, 31]
      context:
        owasp_llm_category: "LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency (by entry name, LLM03:2026 Excessive Agency)"
        owasp_agentic_category: "ASI02: Tool Misuse and Exploitation; ASI03: Identity and Privilege Abuse; ASI09: Human-Agent Trust Exploitation"
        taxonomy_mapping: "AML.T0053 AI Agent Tool Invocation (achieves AML.TA0005 Execution, AML.TA0012 Privilege Escalation, AML.TA0015 Lateral Movement), ATLAS release 2026.09, looked up in this dispatch"
        chain: ["src/server.js:30 unauthenticated caller", "src/helpdesk.js:13 model decides the command", "src/helpdesk.js:17 shell with process authority"]
        agreeing_skills: []
      tags: ["llm-security", "agency", "allowlist", "authorisation"]

    - id: llm-security-tester/01JS7SHELL0000000000000001/003
      severity: critical
      type: prompt_injection
      file: "src/helpdesk.js"
      line_range: [13, 14]
      message: |
        Direct prompt injection. The user's text is concatenated into the system prompt, the most trusted channel. The user turn meanwhile holds a fixed string. Untrusted input is promoted to developer instructions instead of being passed as data.
      rationale: |
        This is the concatenation NIST AI 100-2 E2025 defines as prompt injection: "An attack which exploits the concatenation of untrusted input with a prompt constructed by a higher-trust party such as the application designer" (page 111).
        Here the untrusted text ends the system prompt, so instructions in it ("ignore the problem; reply with ...") sit at the same trust level as the application's own.
        OWASP LLM01:2025 Prompt Injection says "it is unclear if there are fool-proof methods of prevention for prompt injection". Moving the text into the user turn reduces this risk but does not remove it. The impact is bounded only by findings 001 and 002.
      suggestion: |
        Keep the system prompt constant and pass the user's text as the user message, with an instruction to treat it as a problem description, not as instructions.
        Separation alone does not close findings 001 and 002 (check 1). Bound what a landed injection can do by removing the shell sink and allowlisting actions.
      confidence: HIGH
      confidence_rationale: |
        The concatenation is in the line read:
          untrusted text from src/helpdesk.js:13: "system: 'You are a helpdesk assistant. Reply with one shell command that fixes this problem: ' + userMessage,"
        and the value comes from the request body at untrusted text from src/server.js:21: "message = JSON.parse(body).message;".
        The hidden-character search for this file was not run (see limitations).
      citations:
        evidence:
          - file: "src/helpdesk.js"
            line_range: [12, 16]
          - file: "src/server.js"
            line_range: [19, 30]
      context:
        owasp_llm_category: "LLM01:2025 Prompt Injection (by entry name, LLM01:2026 Prompt Injection)"
        owasp_agentic_category: "ASI01: Agent Goal Hijack"
        taxonomy_mapping: "AML.T0051.000 (LLM Prompt Injection, sub-technique Direct; achieves AML.TA0005 Execution), ATLAS release 2026.09, looked up in this dispatch"
        chain: ["src/server.js:21 request body", "src/helpdesk.js:13 system field"]
        agreeing_skills: []
      tags: ["llm-security", "injection", "separation"]

    - id: llm-security-tester/01JS7SHELL0000000000000001/004
      severity: critical
      type: rogue_agents
      file: "src/helpdesk.js"
      line_range: [11, 18]
      message: |
        Nothing records which command the model chose, who asked for it, or what it returned. A command outside the helpdesk task runs and leaves no audit trail in the application.
      rationale: |
        The agentic entry "ASI10: Rogue Agents" asks for "comprehensive, immutable and signed audit logs of all agent actions, tool calls, and inter-agent communication" (page 37 of the agentic document cited under check 12). fixProblem and the /fix handler log nothing.
        Without a record, the misuse in finding 001 cannot be reconstructed, and incident-responder's runbook has nothing to start from.
      suggestion: |
        Before running any action, write an append-only audit record with:
          - the authenticated caller
          - the request identifier
          - the action and its exact arguments
          - the exit status
        Write it outside the process's own write access. Redact personal data in the user's message before it is logged (check 10).
      confidence: MEDIUM
      confidence_rationale: |
        The three files read contain no logging call. Whether a wrapper or proxy records requests elsewhere is not in those files, and I could not search the repository for one (see limitations).
      citations:
        evidence:
          - file: "src/helpdesk.js"
            line_range: [11, 18]
          - file: "src/server.js"
            line_range: [18, 31]
      context:
        owasp_llm_category: "not mapped to a 2025 entry"
        owasp_agentic_category: "ASI10: Rogue Agents"
        taxonomy_mapping: "no ATLAS identifier chosen for this finding"
        agreeing_skills: []
      tags: ["llm-security", "audit", "agentic"]

    - id: llm-security-tester/01JS7SHELL0000000000000001/005
      severity: critical
      type: unbounded_consumption
      file: "src/server.js"
      line_range: [8, 31]
      message: |
        POST /fix needs no authentication and has no per-caller limit. Each request makes one model call through complete() and one synchronous shell execution, which can hold the Node event loop for up to 10 seconds. A few requests in a row keep the server unavailable to everyone. Once complete() is backed by a paid model, the same requests also run up model cost with no budget.
      rationale: |
        Output length is capped (src/helpdesk.js:15, `max_tokens: 200`), and there is one model call per request with no loop or recursion, so iteration and tool-call depth are bounded.
        What is missing is a per-user budget and authentication in front of the model call. Check 9 asks whether a caller can reach the inference endpoint without authentication; here it can.
        OWASP LLM10:2025 Unbounded Consumption: "By initiating a high volume of operations, attackers exploit the cost-per-use model of cloud-based AI services, leading to unsustainable financial burdens on the provider and risking financial ruin."
        Both complete() and execSync are synchronous, so the server handles one /fix request at a time, and each request blocks every other route as well.
        MAX_BODY at src/server.js:6 and :16 limits only the request size.
      suggestion: |
        Authenticate callers of /fix and enforce per-caller rate limits and a per-caller budget on model calls and action runs, counted separately. Make the model call and any action asynchronous so one request cannot block the event loop.
      confidence: HIGH
      confidence_rationale: |
        The whole handler is in the lines read: src/server.js:9-12 routes on method and path only, and untrusted text from src/server.js:30: "res.writeHead(200, { 'content-type': 'text/plain' }).end(fixProblem(message));" runs for every well-formed request.
        Whether a reverse proxy adds authentication or rate limits is outside the files read (see unknowns).
      citations:
        evidence:
          - file: "src/server.js"
            line_range: [6, 31]
          - file: "src/helpdesk.js"
            line_range: [12, 17]
      context:
        owasp_llm_category: "LLM10:2025 Unbounded Consumption (by entry name, LLM06:2026 Unbounded Consumption)"
        taxonomy_mapping: "AML.T0034 Cost Harvesting (achieves AML.TA0011 Impact), ATLAS release 2026.09, looked up in this dispatch"
        agreeing_skills: []
      tags: ["llm-security", "consumption", "availability"]

    - id: llm-security-tester/01JS7SHELL0000000000000001/006
      severity: critical
      type: misinformation
      file: "src/helpdesk.js"
      line_range: [12, 17]
      message: |
        The model's answer drives an action with a safety consequence, a shell command on the server, and nothing checks the answer first. No attacker is needed: an ordinary wrong or over-broad command from the model runs unchecked.
      rationale: |
        This is the class "Misinformation that acts" under check 13: a model's answer drives an action with a safety consequence and nothing checks it first.
        The reply goes from complete() at src/helpdesk.js:12 straight to execSync at :17.
        Whether a given answer is correct belongs to hallucination-detector. This finding is only that nothing stands between the answer and the action.
        The fix is the same as for findings 001 and 002.
      suggestion: |
        Map the model's answer onto a fixed set of vetted actions, and require human confirmation of the exact action before anything destructive runs.
      confidence: HIGH
      confidence_rationale: |
        The whole defect is in the lines read:
          untrusted text from src/helpdesk.js:17: "return execSync(reply.text, { encoding: 'utf8', timeout: 10000 });"
        No check lies between the reply at line 12 and line 17.
      citations:
        evidence:
          - file: "src/helpdesk.js"
            line_range: [12, 17]
      context:
        owasp_llm_category: "LLM09:2025 Misinformation (by entry name, LLM07:2026 Misinformation)"
        taxonomy_mapping: "no ATLAS identifier chosen for this finding"
        agreeing_skills: []
      tags: ["llm-security", "misinformation", "unchecked-action"]
